L6: # ERC-8196: AI Agent Authenticated Wallet
L7: 
L8: ### Policy-bound transaction execution and verifiable credential delegation for autonomous AI agents
L9: 
L10: Authors  | Leigh Cronian (@cybercentry) <leigh.cronian@cybercentry.co.uk>, Chris Johnson <chris@virtuals.io>

L28: ## Abstract
L29: 
L30: This ERC defines a standard interface for AI agent-authenticated wallets. These wallets execute transactions only when accompanied by verifiable cryptographic proof that the action complies with a specific policy defined by the asset owner.
L31: 
L32: It serves as Layer 2 (Execute) in a modular trust stack designed for secure autonomous AI agents:
L33:   * Layer 1 (Identify and Verify): 【12†ERC-8126】 - identification, verification and risk scoring
L34:   * Layer 2 (Execute): 【26†ERC-8196】 - policy-bound execution with immutable audit trail
L35: The design enables secure credential delegation without exposing private keys, prevents host manipulation of agent behavior, provides tamper-evident logging of all session activity, and ensures users retain final say over their agents and actions, as emphasized in the EF Mandate (“a user has the final say over their identities, assets, actions, and agents”).

L20: # Proof-of-Behavior Protocol for Autonomous AI Agents
L21: ## 【1†Abstract】
L22: 
L23: Autonomous AI agents execute actions — file writes, API calls, shell commands — on behalf of human principals. No standard mechanism exists for a third party to verify that an agent acted within its declared behavioral rules, that policy enforcement occurred before execution (not after), or that the action log has not been tampered with after the fact.【2†¶】
L24: This document defines the Proof-of-Behavior (PoB) protocol: a minimal, language-agnostic standard for tamper-evident audit trails and pre-execution policy enforcement in AI agent systems. The protocol specifies a signed receipt format, a hash-chain linking scheme, a policy gate contract, and a cross-agent reference mechanism.【3†¶】

L650: The receipts of the permission's own agent form one chain, and those under each delegation another. In each chain, in log order, the first has "seq" 0. Each later one has the next "seq" and names the one before in "previous" (chain-broken), and is not dated before it (time-went-backwards). A receipt with a problem keeps its place in its chain, provided its content could be read and the records it relies on were found: the next receipt is checked against it. So one break is reported once.【296†¶】
L651: A countersignature has exactly the content {"stub": the receipt's digest, "type": "provared.countersignature.v0", "when": a time}, and states that the action took place with the service. It is carried in the receipt's log entry and signed with the key set the permission gives for the service the receipt names in "with". A verifier MUST confirm "stub" (countersignature-wrong-stub), that such keys exist (countersignature-not-possible), and both signatures (countersignature-invalid).
L652: A receipt without a countersignature is one-sided. This is a reported state, not a problem: such a receipt shows only what the agent stated.【297†¶】
L653: Where an executor (【5†Section 2】) is to countersign, a receipt names the executor in "with", since a countersignature is verified with the keys that the permission gives for the service the receipt names. The party beyond the executor, if there is one, is then not named in "with", and the permission's "with" does not limit which such parties the agent deals with; a reserved document name such as "provared.http-request" can bind the receipt to the call the executor made.
L654: Where that party countersigns instead, the receipt names it, and the executor is not named.【298†¶】
L655: An approval is the principal's approval of exactly one action. Its content holds exactly "type" ("provared.approval.v0"), "id", "slip", "action", and "when", and optionally "amount", "with", and "details". It is signed with the permission's passkey and carried in the receipt's entry, and the receipt names it by its digest. The receipt MUST name the approval in its entry (approval-mismatch), and an approval it names MUST be there (approval-not-found).
L656: The approval's "slip", "action", "amount", "with", and "details" MUST match the receipt's, each present in both or neither (approval-mismatch). Its "id" MUST NOT be that of an approval in an earlier entry (approval-reused) or of another record (duplicate-id). Its passkey signature MUST verify against the permission's "issuer" (approval-invalid). It MUST NOT be dated more than 300 seconds after the receipt, which was signed after it (approval-dated-after-stub).
L657: An approval shows that the passkey approved the action, not that the principal read it.【299†¶】

The executor records one-time use in shared atomic state; the receipt, which carries a log inclusion proof, can be verified offline.
L936: That document states that it provides no offline or cross-domain double-spend prevention, and that a committed operation is not verifiable evidence unless a signed record covers it; Section 13 of that document lists what such evidence should hold. Together, the two EMILIA documents provide enforcement before an action takes effect, in the executor's atomic state, and evidence of what was authorized, in the authorization receipt.

L938: The difference is where the limits live and who checks them: there, the executor's store refuses an operation; here, the principal's passkey signs the limits, which may also bound single amounts, counts, and periods and set conditions, each action is a signed receipt that the service may countersign, and any verifier decides afterward, from the records alone, whether each action stayed within the permission.
L939: This document does not stop an action when it is attempted, and an action for which no receipt was written is found only in another party's records (【6†Section 18】). The two designs could be combined: an executor (【5†Section 2】) that refuses an operation before it takes effect, and receipts from which any verifier can later check each action against the limits the principal signed.【444†¶】

L1005: What the head adds is that the permission, as it stands in the log, cannot be replaced afterward by anyone without the recorder's keys, even if its passkey signature later becomes forgeable; it does not make the principal's signature post-quantum.【495†¶】

L1011: With no trusted keys named, "intact" means only that the log is consistent with itself. Anyone can make such a log.【497†¶】
L1012:

L1014: Omission, one side's word:
L1015: An agent that writes no receipt leaves no trace in its own log, and no check of that log shows the gap. Only another party's records can show it: a countersignature kept by the service, or the records of an executor (【5†Section 2】) that refuses any action the permission does not allow, or any action without a verified approval, and records each action it allows (the strongest class of [【442†I-D.schrock-ep-authorization-receipts】] has such an executor, which checks that document's own authorizations).
L1016: An executor's records show the gap only if the action cannot take place without the executor, and if the executor keeps them where the agent's side cannot change them. A permission whose "with" names no service but the executor, and that requires a countersignature for every action, makes each receipt in the log that lacks the executor's countersignature a finding (countersignature-missing, or party-not-allowed for a receipt that names another party).
L1017: A receipt that was never written is found only by comparing the executor's own records with the log, which this document does not specify. A cancellation the principal signed can be left out of the log by whoever keeps it, after which every later receipt reads as within the permission; only the principal's own copy of the cancellation, handed to the verifier (【321†Section 22†github.com】 of [【135†FORMAT】], out of scope here), answers this.
L1018: A one-sided receipt, an acknowledgement, and the times stated in records, on which period limits depend, rest on the signer's own statement.【498†¶】

L1023: The last head, with everything after it, can be removed unnoticed unless someone else holds that head. A recorder can keep two logs that differ after some entry, with heads for each; no consistency proof is defined. Handing heads to others lets them be compared.【499†¶】

L1027: approval-reused and duplicate-id hold within one log, and so do totals, counts, and periods. Receipts for one permission written into two logs, or into a log that was started afresh, are not added together: each log can be within its limits while the two together are not. A recorder that keeps one log for each permission avoids this; the format does not close it.【500†¶】

L1031: The keys of a service in "with" are stated by the principal. A countersignature shows that a holder of those keys signed; it does not show who that holder is. A principal who lists keys they control can countersign their own agent's receipts. A compromise of a service's keys lets anyone countersign in its name: a countersignature is only as strong as the service's keys.【501†¶】

L181: 【37†2020】) has been proposed to record interaction histories and derive reputation scores. More broadly, Salah et al. (【33†2019】) survey the intersection of blockchain and AI, identifying accountability and provenance as key open challenges.
L182: Existing multi-agent systems typically assume cooperative behavior and lack formal mechanisms for identity verification or on-chain governance enforcement. While decentralized identity standards such as DIDs and VCs have been applied to human-centric scenarios, their integration into agentic AI ecosystems as a dynamic trust infrastructure remains underexplored, with security, privacy, and accountability identified as key open challenges (Romandini et al. 【38†2025】).
L183: Our framework addresses this gap by providing a blockchain-based trust anchor that unifies identity binding, authorization enforcement, and interaction-driven reputation management as first-class infrastructure properties.
L184: ## ARCHITECTURE
L185: The proposed framework uses the blockchain as a trust anchor for autonomous multi-agent systems, combining off-chain components responsible for agentic orchestration with on-chain components responsible for identity management, capability discovery, reputation tracking, and governance. Figure 【39†1】 depicts the proposed framework by combining its layered architecture with the seven-step agent interaction lifecycle. The system is organized into three horizontal layers.
L186: The Agent Layer supports off-chain agent orchestration and communication, with agents operating through DIDs provisioned by authorized operators. The Trust Layer, anchored on a blockchain, provides the core trust infrastructure, including the Agent Registry for capability discovery, VC-based endorsements, and reputation management. Smart-contract logic is executed within the blockchain infrastructure to update trust scores and apply incentives or penalties.
L187: Finally, the Oversight Layer enables human supervision, auditing, and intervention over the ecosystem.

L191: 
L192: Layered architecture and agent interaction lifecycle of the proposed framework.
L193: The agent interaction lifecycle unfolds across these layers as follows: (i) each agent is assigned a DID by an authorized operator, who registers it on-chain together with any initial VCs; (ii) agents discover and filter each other through the registry based on capability and reputation; (iii) credentials are verified before interaction begins; (iv) task execution occurs and behavioral outcomes are observed; (v) interacting agents issue VC endorsements for each other; (vi) reputation management updates trust scores and feeds endorsements into future discovery; and (vii) human supervisors monitor the ecosystem, audit trust updates, and intervene when needed.
L194: ### Agent layer and cryptographic identity binding
L195: 
L196: The Agent Layer manages all operational logic: task planning, tool invocation, subagent delegation, and interagent communication. Agents interact through structured protocols such as A2A, which define standardized message formats and delegation workflows that preserve modularity and interoperability. This layer is entirely off-chain, which ensures flexibility and performance without incurring blockchain latency during routine computation.
